John Paul II.bio: John Paul II, born Karol Wojtyła in Poland, was pope of the Roman Catholic Church from 1978 to 2005, one of the longest pontificates in history. A former actor and philosopher, his travels, writings and role in the fall of European communism made him a global moral figure.

Leslie Marmon Silko.bio: Laguna Pueblo novelist and storyteller whose Ceremony (1977) is a central work of Native American literature. Her writing weaves story, land, memory and healing into a single fabric, in the Pueblo oral tradition.

Mario Benedetti.bio: Uruguayan poet, novelist and journalist, author of The Truce and beloved poems like 'No te rindas' (Don't Give Up). Exiled during Uruguay's dictatorship, he wrote of ordinary people's loves, offices and quiet resilience.

Wang Yangming.bio: Wang Yangming was a Chinese Ming-dynasty philosopher, general, and calligrapher, founder of the School of Mind within Neo-Confucianism. He taught the unity of knowledge and action: to truly know something is to put it into practice.

Abdurrahman Wahid.bio: Abdurrahman Wahid, known as Gus Dur, was an Indonesian Muslim scholar, leader of Nahdlatul Ulama, and Indonesia's fourth president. A defender of pluralism and minorities, he is remembered for the quip that God does not need to be defended.

Saadi Shirazi.bio: Persian poet famed for the Gulistan and Bustan, collections of wisdom, ethics and storytelling that are still widely read today.

Sapardi Djoko Damono.bio: Sapardi Djoko Damono was an Indonesian poet beloved for lyrical, deceptively simple verse, including the collection Hujan Bulan Juni ('June Rain'). His line 'what perishes is time; we are eternal' is quoted across Indonesia.

Margaret Atwood.bio: Margaret Atwood is a Canadian novelist, poet and essayist best known for The Handmaid's Tale, her dystopian novel that became a global cultural phenomenon. She has twice won the Booker Prize, for The Blind Assassin and The Testaments.

Gustave Flaubert.bio: Gustave Flaubert was a French novelist who pursued perfection of style with legendary discipline, rewriting pages until every word seemed inevitable. His Madame Bovary, prosecuted for obscenity in 1857, is a landmark of literary realism.

Zora Neale Hurston.bio: Zora Neale Hurston was an American writer and anthropologist at the heart of the Harlem Renaissance, celebrated for her novel Their Eyes Were Watching God. Trained under Franz Boas, she documented the folklore, music and speech of the rural Black South.

Susan B. Anthony.bio: Susan B. Anthony spent more than fifty years campaigning for women's right to vote, co-founding the National Woman Suffrage Association with Elizabeth Cady Stanton. Arrested for voting in 1872, she died fourteen years before the Nineteenth Amendment finally secured women's suffrage.

Ovid.bio: Ovid was a Roman poet celebrated for the Metamorphoses, a vast narrative poem of mythological transformations. Exiled by the emperor Augustus to the Black Sea coast, he spent his last decade writing poems of lament and endurance.

Thomas Paine.bio: Thomas Paine was an English-born political writer whose pamphlet Common Sense in 1776 galvanised the American Revolution. His Rights of Man defended the French Revolution against Burke, and his works made him one of the most influential pamphleteers in history.

Zhuangzi.bio: Zhuangzi was a Chinese Taoist philosopher of the Warring States period, second only to Lao Tzu in the Taoist tradition. His book, the Zhuangzi, mixes parables, dialogues, and dreams to argue for freedom from convention and care.

Immanuel Kant.bio: Immanuel Kant was a German philosopher whose Critique of Pure Reason reshaped modern philosophy by examining the limits of human knowledge. His moral philosophy grounded duty in reason and human dignity, and his essays championed enlightenment and perpetual peace.

bell hooks.bio: bell hooks, born Gloria Jean Watkins, was an American author and feminist theorist who wrote more than thirty books on race, gender, class and love, including Ain't I a Woman and All About Love. She styled her pen name, taken from her great-grandmother, in lowercase to keep the focus on her ideas.

Kenji Miyazawa.bio: Kenji Miyazawa was a Japanese poet and children's author from Iwate whose work was little known in his lifetime and beloved after it. His poem 'Be Not Defeated by the Rain' is recited across Japan as a portrait of quiet endurance.

Robert Louis Stevenson.bio: Robert Louis Stevenson was a Scottish novelist and travel writer, author of Treasure Island, Kidnapped and the Strange Case of Dr Jekyll and Mr Hyde. Plagued by ill health, he travelled restlessly and settled at last in Samoa, where he died at forty-four.

Marcus Garvey.bio: Jamaican publisher and Pan-African leader who founded the Universal Negro Improvement Association. His call for Black pride, self-reliance and African unity influenced liberation movements across the world.

Molière.bio: Molière, born Jean-Baptiste Poquelin, was a French playwright and actor considered the greatest master of comedy in French literature. Tartuffe, The Misanthrope and The Imaginary Invalid satirise hypocrisy and pretension with undiminished freshness.

Tao Yuanming.bio: Tao Yuanming was a Chinese poet who gave up a government career to farm and write in the countryside. His 'Peach Blossom Spring' and drinking poems made him the patron saint of the simple, self-chosen life.

Democritus.bio: Democritus was a Greek philosopher who, with Leucippus, developed the atomic theory of the universe. He held that reality consists of indivisible atoms moving in empty space, and was known in antiquity as the laughing philosopher.

Ralph Waldo Emerson.bio: Ralph Waldo Emerson was an American essayist and philosopher who led the Transcendentalist movement, arguing for self-reliance, intuition and the spiritual presence in nature. His essays 'Nature' and 'Self-Reliance' shaped American thought, and he mentored both Thoreau and Whitman.

John Stuart Mill.bio: John Stuart Mill was an English philosopher and political economist, the most influential liberal thinker of the 19th century. On Liberty defended individual freedom against social coercion, and his Autobiography candidly records his extraordinary education and mental crisis.

Clarice Lispector.bio: Brazilian novelist and short-story writer born in Ukraine, famed for the stream-of-consciousness of Near to the Wild Heart, The Passion According to G.H. and Água Viva. Her intense, interior prose made her one of Brazil's most original voices.

Bulleh Shah.bio: Punjabi Sufi poet and humanist. His kafis challenge religious ritualism and caste, and are still widely sung today.

Yoko Ono.bio: Yoko Ono is a Japanese artist, musician, and peace activist, a pioneer of conceptual art whose instruction pieces in Grapefruit invited audiences to complete the work in their imagination. She was married to John Lennon.

Kabir.bio: Indian mystic poet and saint whose dohas challenged religious orthodoxy. He is revered by Hindus, Muslims and Sikhs alike, and his verses are included in the Sikh scriptures.

Gabriel García Márquez.bio: Colombian novelist and journalist, pioneer of magical realism and winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature (1982). His masterpiece One Hundred Years of Solitude is one of the most translated and beloved novels of the twentieth century.

Derek Walcott.bio: Saint Lucian poet and playwright who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1992. His epic poem Omeros reimagined Homer's world in the Caribbean, and his work gave the islands' landscapes, history and Creole voices a central place in world poetry.

Epicurus.bio: Epicurus was a Greek philosopher who founded a school in Athens known as the Garden. He taught that pleasure, rightly understood as freedom from pain and fear, comes from friendship, simplicity and philosophy rather than luxury.

Pablo Neruda.bio: Chilean poet and diplomat, winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature (1971), celebrated for Twenty Love Poems and the Song of Despair and the epic Canto General. His verses of love, nature and political hope are recited across the Spanish-speaking world.

Sri Aurobindo.bio: Indian philosopher, yogi and nationalist. He founded the integral yoga movement and the Sri Aurobindo Ashram in Pondicherry.

Su Shi.bio: Su Shi, also known as Su Dongpo, was a Song-dynasty poet, essayist, calligrapher, and statesman. Exiled repeatedly for his outspokenness, he answered misfortune with some of the most joyful and philosophical verse in Chinese literature.

Anton Chekhov.bio: Anton Chekhov was a Russian playwright and master of the short story, a practising doctor who wrote The Cherry Orchard, Uncle Vanya and hundreds of stories. His restrained, humane art reshaped both the theatre and short fiction of the 20th century.

Yunus Emre.bio: Turkish folk poet and Sufi, a central voice of Anatolian humanism writing in simple, powerful Turkish verse.

Leonardo da Vinci.bio: Leonardo da Vinci was an Italian Renaissance painter, engineer and anatomist whose notebooks reveal an insatiable curiosity about nature and art. He painted the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, and filled thousands of pages with studies, inventions and observations.

Charles Eastman.bio: Dakota (Santee Sioux) physician and writer, known by his Dakota name Ohiyesa. Books such as The Soul of the Indian interpreted Native spirituality, silence and values for a wide readership in the early twentieth century.

Rabia al-Adawiyya.bio: Muslim saint and Sufi mystic of Basra, one of the earliest voices of divine love in Islamic mysticism.

Nazim Hikmet.bio: Turkish poet often called the 'romantic revolutionary'; imprisoned for his politics, he wrote some of Turkish literature's most loved poems.

Salvador Dalí.bio: Salvador Dalí was a Spanish Surrealist artist famous for dreamlike images such as the melting clocks of The Persistence of Memory. A brilliant self-publicist and technician, he worked in painting, film, sculpture and design from his base in Catalonia.

Muhammad Iqbal.bio: Philosopher, poet and politician of British India, writing in Persian and Urdu. His ideas inspired the Pakistan movement and his poetry is revered across South Asia.

Ibn Arabi.bio: Andalusian Sufi philosopher and poet who developed the doctrine of the unity of being (wahdat al-wujud).

Ryunosuke Satoro.bio: Ryunosuke Satoro is a Japanese poet whose brief verses on togetherness and the natural world are quoted around the world. His best-known lines compare individuals to single drops of water and humanity to an ocean.

Federico García Lorca.bio: Federico García Lorca was a Spanish poet and playwright, author of the Gypsy Ballads and the tragedies Blood Wedding and The House of Bernarda Alba. He was murdered by Nationalist forces at the start of the Spanish Civil War, at thirty-eight.

Julius Nyerere.bio: Julius Nyerere led Tanganyika to independence in 1961 and became the first president of Tanzania. Known as Mwalimu, 'the teacher', he championed education, equality and African socialism.

Haruki Murakami.bio: Haruki Murakami is a Japanese novelist whose surreal, melancholic books — Norwegian Wood, Kafka on the Shore, and 1Q84 among them — have been translated into more than fifty languages. He is also a devoted marathon runner.

Roald Dahl.bio: Roald Dahl was a British author of Norwegian parentage whose children's books, including Charlie and the Chocolate Factory, Matilda and The BFG, have sold hundreds of millions of copies. Before writing he served as an RAF fighter pilot and intelligence officer.

Dag Hammarskjöld.bio: Dag Hammarskjöld was a Swedish diplomat who served as the second Secretary-General of the United Nations from 1953 until his death in a plane crash during a peace mission to the Congo. He was posthumously awarded the Nobel Peace Prize; his spiritual journal Markings was published after his death.

Charles Reade.bio: Charles Reade was an English novelist and dramatist whose The Cloister and the Hearth is a richly researched tale of 15th-century Europe. A meticulous collector of facts and documents, he campaigned through his fiction against abuses in prisons and asylums.

Al-Biruni.bio: Persian scholar of the Islamic Golden Age: astronomer, mathematician and one of the first anthropologists to study India.

Forough Farrokhzad.bio: Pioneering Iranian modernist poet whose bold, personal voice transformed Persian poetry.

Shunryu Suzuki.bio: Shunryu Suzuki was a Japanese Soto Zen master who founded the San Francisco Zen Center and helped establish Zen in America. His book Zen Mind, Beginner's Mind is one of the most loved introductions to Zen practice.

Akka Mahadevi.bio: Kannada poet-saint of the Bhakti movement. Her vachanas express fierce devotion and social defiance.

Sheng Yen.bio: Sheng Yen was a Taiwanese Chan (Zen) Buddhist master and scholar who founded Dharma Drum Mountain. He popularized a practical way through difficulty: face it, accept it, deal with it, then let it go.

Ryokan.bio: Ryokan was a Japanese Zen monk who lived as a hermit in a small hut, writing gentle poems and playing with village children. Offered charity all his life, he owned almost nothing and is remembered for his warmth and simplicity.

Hans Christian Andersen.bio: Hans Christian Andersen was a Danish author whose fairy tales, including The Little Mermaid, The Ugly Duckling and The Emperor's New Clothes, are beloved in every language. Born to poverty in Odense, he travelled widely and drew on his journeys throughout his writing.

Lung Ying-tai.bio: Lung Ying-tai is a Taiwanese writer and essayist, and served as Taiwan's first Minister of Culture. Her book of essays on family, Mu Song ('Watching You Go'), moved readers across the Chinese-speaking world.

Toussaint Louverture.bio: Formerly enslaved leader of the Haitian Revolution who defeated French, Spanish and British forces and abolished slavery in Saint-Domingue. His generalship and statecraft laid the ground for Haiti, the first free Black republic.

George Sand.bio: George Sand, the pen name of Amandine Dupin, was a French novelist and journalist who scandalised and fascinated 19th-century Paris. Her novels of love and rural life, and her independent personal life, made her one of the most notable women writers of her century.

Thomas Mann.bio: Thomas Mann was a German novelist whose Buddenbrooks, The Magic Mountain and Death in Venice dissect European bourgeois culture with irony and depth. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1929 and spent the Nazi years in exile, broadcasting against Hitler from America.

Baruch Spinoza.bio: Baruch Spinoza was a Dutch philosopher of Portuguese-Jewish descent who ground lenses for a living while writing works that reshaped philosophy. Expelled from his synagogue for his views, he argued in the Ethics for a rational, pantheistic understanding of God and nature.

Julian of Norwich.bio: Julian of Norwich was an English anchoress who lived in a cell attached to a church in Norwich and wrote the earliest surviving book in English by a woman. Her Revelations of Divine Love, recording visions she received during a grave illness, is famed for its message of hope.

Akira Kurosawa.bio: Akira Kurosawa was a Japanese film director whose works — Rashomon, Seven Samurai, and Ran — reshaped world cinema. His films pair humanist storytelling with some of the most influential images ever put on screen.

Al-Ghazali.bio: Persian theologian, philosopher and mystic, one of the most influential Muslim scholars, known as 'the Proof of Islam.'

Michelangelo.bio: Michelangelo Buonarroti was an Italian Renaissance sculptor, painter and architect regarded as one of the greatest artists in history. He carved the David and the Pietà and painted the ceiling of the Sistine Chapel in Rome.

Plutarch.bio: Plutarch was a Greek biographer and essayist who lived under Roman rule. His Parallel Lives paired famous Greeks and Romans to draw moral lessons, and his Moralia essays range across philosophy, religion and everyday conduct.

Jean Rhys.bio: Novelist born in Dominica, best known for Wide Sargasso Sea, her haunting prequel to Jane Eyre told from a Caribbean Creole woman's perspective. Her spare prose gave voice to women living on the margins of empire.

Basava.bio: Indian philosopher and social reformer, founder of the Lingayat movement and pioneer of the Kannada vachana tradition.

Ben Okri.bio: Ben Okri is a Nigerian poet and novelist whose novel The Famished Road won the Booker Prize in 1991. His lyrical work blends everyday realism with the spirit world of West African storytelling.

N. Scott Momaday.bio: Kiowa novelist, poet and essayist who won the Pulitzer Prize for House Made of Dawn in 1969, a landmark that launched the Native American Renaissance. His essays in The Man Made of Words explore language, story and identity.

Wen Tianxiang.bio: Wen Tianxiang was a Song-dynasty scholar-official and poet who refused to serve the Mongol conquerors and was executed after years in prison. His 'Song of Righteousness' and his prison poems made him a lasting symbol of loyalty.

Aimé Césaire.bio: Martinican poet and politician who co-founded the Negritude movement with Leopold Senghor and Leon Damas. His Notebook of a Return to the Native Land is a landmark of anti-colonial poetry, written in a surge of surrealist imagery.

Gabriela Mistral.bio: Chilean poet, educator and diplomat who in 1945 became the first Latin American to win the Nobel Prize in Literature. Her collections Desolación and Ternura sing of motherhood, children, nature and the rural poor she spent her life teaching.

Qian Zhongshu.bio: Qian Zhongshu was a Chinese scholar and novelist best known for Fortress Besieged (1947), a witty satire of intellectuals in wartime China and one of the great Chinese novels of the twentieth century.

Aesop.bio: Aesop was a storyteller of ancient Greece, traditionally said to have been an enslaved man who won freedom through his wit. The animal fables credited to him, such as The Tortoise and the Hare, have taught moral lessons for over two millennia.

Yamamoto Tsunetomo.bio: Yamamoto Tsunetomo was a Japanese samurai of the Nabeshima clan whose spoken reflections were recorded as the Hagakure, a guide to the way of the warrior centered on devotion and living fully in the present moment.

C. S. Lewis.bio: C. S. Lewis was an Irish-born scholar and writer at Oxford, author of The Chronicles of Narnia, Mere Christianity and The Screwtape Letters. A close friend of Tolkien, he moved from atheism to Christianity and became one of its most popular modern interpreters.

Rainer Maria Rilke.bio: Rainer Maria Rilke was an Austrian poet born in Prague, author of the Duino Elegies and the Sonnets to Orpheus. His Letters to a Young Poet, advising patience and solitude, have guided generations of artists; he wrote in German and later in French.

Émile Zola.bio: Émile Zola was a French novelist and the leading figure of literary naturalism, whose twenty-volume Rougon-Macquart cycle traces a family through the Second Empire. His open letter J'Accuse...! in defence of Alfred Dreyfus became a landmark of political journalism.

Joy Harjo.bio: Muscogee (Creek) poet, musician and author who served three terms as United States Poet Laureate, the first Native American to hold the post. Poems such as Remember call readers back to sky, earth and ancestry.

Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz.bio: Mexican Hieronymite nun, poet and scholar of the colonial Baroque, famed for the philosophical poem 'Primero sueño' and her bold defence of women's right to learn in the Reply to Sor Filotea. She is celebrated as the first great poet of the Americas.

Marie Curie.bio: Marie Curie was a Polish-born physicist and chemist who pioneered the study of radioactivity, a term she coined. She remains the only person to win Nobel Prizes in two different sciences — Physics in 1903 and Chemistry in 1911 — and died of illness caused by her long exposure to radiation.

Anatole France.bio: Anatole France was a French novelist, critic and man of letters, one of the most respected French writers of his era. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1921; his ironic, humane novels include Penguin Island and The Gods Are Athirst.

Nikos Kazantzakis.bio: Nikos Kazantzakis was a Greek writer from Crete, author of Zorba the Greek and The Last Temptation of Christ. A restless traveller and seeker, he also produced a vast modern sequel to the Odyssey; his epitaph reads 'I hope nothing. I fear nothing. I am free.'

Manuel L. Quezon.bio: Manuel L. Quezon was the first president of the Commonwealth of the Philippines, remembered as the father of the national language. His blunt declaration that he would rather have a government run like hell by Filipinos than like heaven by Americans became famous.

Jorge Luis Borges.bio: Argentine short-story writer, essayist and poet whose labyrinthine tales in Ficciones and The Aleph reshaped modern literature. Director of Argentina's National Library, he explored time, infinity and invented worlds with unmatched precision.

Kamau Brathwaite.bio: Barbadian poet and historian whose idea of 'nation language' reshaped Caribbean poetry. He argued its rhythms should follow the hurricane and the calypso rather than the English pentameter, and he chronicled African retentions in Caribbean culture.

Frida Kahlo.bio: Mexican painter famed for raw, symbolic self-portraits that turned a life of pain after a devastating bus accident into art of extraordinary power. Her diary and letters, like her paintings, are celebrated for their honesty and defiance.

Okakura Kakuzo.bio: Okakura Kakuzo was a Japanese scholar who worked to preserve Japan's traditional arts and explained Asian culture to the West. His Book of Tea (1906), written in English, remains a classic meditation on simplicity and beauty.

Arthur Schopenhauer.bio: Arthur Schopenhauer was a German philosopher whose major work, The World as Will and Representation, portrayed life as driven by blind striving. Long neglected, his pessimistic yet lucid philosophy later influenced Tolstoy, Wagner, Nietzsche and many artists.

Jamaica Kincaid.bio: Antiguan-born writer known for A Small Place, her fierce indictment of tourism and colonialism, and for novels such as Annie John and Lucy. Her lyrical, unflinching prose explores Antigua, family, gardens and the long shadow of empire.

Cicero.bio: Marcus Tullius Cicero was a Roman statesman, lawyer and orator considered the master of Latin prose. His speeches, letters and philosophical works, including On Friendship, transmitted Greek philosophy to the Roman world.

Alexandre Dumas.bio: Alexandre Dumas was a French novelist whose swashbuckling historical adventures, The Three Musketeers and The Count of Monte Cristo, have never been out of print. One of the most widely read French authors in the world, he wrote hundreds of plays, novels and travel books.

Jim Ryun.bio: Jim Ryun is an American former athlete who in 1964 became the first high school student to run a mile in under four minutes. He won a silver medal in the 1500 metres at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics and later served as a US Representative from Kansas.

Samuel Johnson.bio: Samuel Johnson was an English writer who compiled the first great Dictionary of the English Language in 1755. Poet, essayist and the most quoted conversationalist of his age, his life was immortalised in Boswell's famous biography.

Louise Erdrich.bio: Turtle Mountain Chippewa novelist and poet, author of Love Medicine and The Painted Drum. Her interwoven novels chronicle Ojibwe families, land and survival across generations in the northern plains.

Elif Shafak.bio: Turkish-British novelist. Her bestseller The Forty Rules of Love brought Rumi's story to millions of readers.

Jose Rizal.bio: Jose Rizal was a Filipino writer, physician, and polymath whose novels Noli Me Tangere and El Filibusterismo exposed the abuses of Spanish colonial rule. Executed by firing squad in 1896, he became the national hero of the Philippines.

Bai Juyi.bio: Bai Juyi was a Tang-dynasty Chinese poet famous for verse so plainspoken that, legend says, he read each poem to an old washerwoman and rewrote whatever she could not understand. His 'Song of Everlasting Regret' remains beloved across East Asia.

Cheng Yen.bio: Cheng Yen is a Taiwanese Buddhist nun who founded the Tzu Chi Foundation in 1966, now one of the world's largest Buddhist humanitarian organizations. Her 'Still Thoughts' aphorisms teach speaking good words, thinking good thoughts, and doing good deeds.

Julio Cortázar.bio: Argentine novelist and master of the short story, author of the experimental novel Hopscotch (1963) and story collections such as Blow-Up. A central figure of the Latin American Boom, he blended fantasy, play and everyday life.

Sitting Bull.bio: Hunkpapa Lakota leader and holy man who united the Plains tribes in resistance to United States expansion and led them to victory at the Little Bighorn in 1876. He remains an enduring symbol of Indigenous sovereignty and dignity.

Franklin D. Roosevelt.bio: Franklin D. Roosevelt led the United States through the Great Depression with his New Deal programs and through most of the Second World War. He is the only American president elected four times, serving from 1933 until his death in 1945.

Eileen Chang.bio: Eileen Chang was a Chinese writer celebrated for her psychologically sharp fiction of love and war in 1940s Shanghai and Hong Kong, including Lust, Caution and Love in a Fallen City. She later lived in the United States.

Ajahn Chah.bio: Ajahn Chah was a Thai Buddhist monk of the Forest Tradition whose simple, humorous teaching drew students from around the world to his monastery at Wat Nong Pah Pong. His core instruction was letting go.

Amílcar Cabral.bio: Amílcar Cabral was an agronomist and revolutionary who led the liberation movement of Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde against Portuguese colonial rule. He was assassinated in 1973, months before Guinea-Bissau declared independence.

Hafez.bio: Persian lyric poet of Shiraz. His Divan of ghazals is among the most beloved works in all of Persian literature.

Hsing Yun.bio: Hsing Yun was a Chinese Buddhist monk who founded the Fo Guang Shan monastery and the Buddha's Light International Association in Taiwan. He promoted 'Humanistic Buddhism' and his 'four givings': confidence, joy, hope, and convenience to others.

Albert Schweitzer.bio: Albert Schweitzer was an Alsatian theologian, musician and physician who founded a hospital at Lambaréné in Gabon and served there for decades. His philosophy of reverence for life and his Bach scholarship earned him the Nobel Peace Prize in 1952.

Chief Joseph.bio: Leader of the Wallowa band of the Nez Perce, famed for his people's 1877 fighting retreat toward Canada and his surrender words, 'I will fight no more forever.' He spent his later years pleading his people's cause in Washington.

Andres Bonifacio.bio: Andres Bonifacio was a Filipino revolutionary who founded the Katipunan, the secret society that launched the Philippine Revolution against Spain in 1896. A warehouse clerk by trade, he was also a poet of fierce love for his homeland.

Dylan Thomas.bio: Dylan Thomas was a Welsh poet whose sonorous, musical verse made him famous on both sides of the Atlantic. Under Milk Wood, his play for voices, and poems such as Fern Hill and Do Not Go Gentle into That Good Night, are classics of 20th-century poetry.

Zhang Zai.bio: Zhang Zai was a Chinese Neo-Confucian philosopher of the Song dynasty. His famous four 'Hengqu Sentences' — setting the heart at rest for Heaven and Earth and opening peace for generations to come — became a creed for Chinese scholars.

Edmund Burke.bio: Edmund Burke was an Irish-born British statesman and political thinker, celebrated as a parliamentary orator. His Reflections on the Revolution in France made him a founding voice of modern conservatism, while he also supported American grievances and prosecuted abuses in India.

Guru Nanak.bio: Founder of Sikhism and the first of the ten Sikh Gurus. He taught the oneness of God and the equality of all people.

Isabel Allende.bio: Chilean-American novelist whose debut The House of the Spirits (1982) became a landmark of magical realism. One of the most widely read Spanish-language authors in the world, she writes sweeping family sagas of love, exile and memory.

Mansur al-Hallaj.bio: Persian Sufi mystic executed in Baghdad for his ecstatic declaration 'Ana al-Haqq' (I am the Truth).

Leonard Cohen.bio: Leonard Cohen was a Canadian singer-songwriter, poet and novelist from Montreal whose songs, including 'Hallelujah,' 'Suzanne' and 'Anthem,' combined spiritual longing with wry, literate wit. He recorded from 1967 until his final album, You Want It Darker, released weeks before his death in 2016.

Che Guevara.bio: Argentine Marxist revolutionary, physician and writer whose journeys across Latin America, recorded in The Motorcycle Diaries, shaped his convictions. A major figure of the Cuban Revolution, his essays and speeches remain widely read and debated.

Liu Cixin.bio: Liu Cixin is a Chinese science-fiction writer, author of the Remembrance of Earth's Past trilogy that begins with The Three-Body Problem. He is the first Asian writer to win the Hugo Award for Best Novel.

Black Elk.bio: Oglala Lakota holy man whose great vision and life story, recorded in Black Elk Speaks, became one of the most widely read accounts of Native American spirituality. He witnessed the Little Bighorn and the Wounded Knee massacre.

Tan Malaka.bio: Tan Malaka was an Indonesian independence activist, philosopher, and writer who spent decades in exile agitating against Dutch colonial rule. His book Madilog argued for reason and materialism as tools of liberation.

Shams Tabrizi.bio: Persian Sufi dervish and the spiritual companion of Rumi, whose meeting transformed Rumi into a poet of ecstasy.

Virgil.bio: Virgil was the foremost poet of ancient Rome, author of the Eclogues, the Georgics and the Aeneid. His epic of Aeneas became Rome's national poem and influenced European literature from Dante onward.

Lu Xun.bio: Lu Xun was China's most influential modern writer, famous for sharp short stories such as Diary of a Madman and The True Story of Ah Q. He abandoned medicine for literature, believing that changing minds mattered more than healing bodies.

A. A. Milne.bio: A. A. Milne was an English author best known for the Winnie-the-Pooh stories, created for his son Christopher Robin and inspired by his stuffed animals. A successful playwright and humourist before Pooh, he also wrote the classic children's poems of When We Were Very Young.

Buddhadasa Bhikkhu.bio: Buddhadasa Bhikkhu was a Thai Buddhist monk and reformer who founded the Suan Mokkh forest monastery. He taught a rational, demythologized Buddhism centered on dependent origination and freedom from clinging to 'I' and 'mine'.

Ralph Ellison.bio: Ralph Ellison was an American novelist from Oklahoma City whose single completed novel, Invisible Man, won the National Book Award in 1953 and became a classic of American literature. Trained first as a jazz musician, he brought a musician's ear to his prose about race and identity.

Du Fu.bio: Du Fu is regarded as China's greatest poet, a Tang-dynasty writer whose work earned him the title 'Poet-Sage'. Writing through war and political collapse, he fused personal hardship with deep compassion for ordinary people.

Nguyen Du.bio: Nguyen Du was a Vietnamese poet whose verse novel The Tale of Kieu is considered the greatest work of Vietnamese literature. Written in the nom script, it tells of a talented young woman sacrificed to fate and family duty.

Bruce Lee.bio: Bruce Lee was a Hong Kong-American martial artist and actor who transformed martial-arts cinema with films such as Enter the Dragon. His philosophy of adaptability — 'be water' — blended Taoist ideas with his own Jeet Kune Do.

Søren Kierkegaard.bio: Søren Kierkegaard was a Danish philosopher and theologian regarded as the first existentialist thinker. Writing under playful pseudonyms, he explored faith, anxiety and the individual's leap beyond rational systems in works such as Fear and Trembling.

Epictetus.bio: Epictetus was a Greek-born slave in Rome who won his freedom and became one of the most influential Stoic teachers. His Discourses and the handbook known as the Enchiridion teach that freedom lies in mastering one's own judgments and desires.

Ibn Sina.bio: Persian polymath of the Islamic Golden Age, known in the West as Avicenna. His Canon of Medicine was a standard medical text in Europe for centuries.

Thomas Aquinas.bio: Thomas Aquinas was an Italian Dominican friar and the foremost scholastic theologian of the Middle Ages. His Summa Theologica attempted a complete rational account of Christian doctrine and remains central to Catholic philosophy.

Eleanor Roosevelt.bio: Eleanor Roosevelt was the longest-serving First Lady of the United States, from 1933 to 1945, and reinvented the role as a platform for civil rights and social reform. Afterward she became a US delegate to the United Nations and chaired the commission that drafted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights.

Bob Marley.bio: Jamaican singer and songwriter who carried reggae and its messages of freedom, faith and unity to the whole world. Songs like Redemption Song and Three Little Birds made him one of the most beloved musical voices of the twentieth century.

Simón Bolívar.bio: Venezuelan military and political leader who led the independence of much of Spanish South America from Spanish rule. His Angostura Address and Jamaica Letter remain foundational texts of Latin American republican thought.

Eduardo Galeano.bio: Uruguayan journalist and writer whose Open Veins of Latin America (1971) retold the continent's history from below. His trilogy Memory of Fire and The Book of Embraces blend history, fable and vignette into a unique literary form.

Matsuo Basho.bio: Matsuo Basho was Japan's greatest haiku master, who raised the short comic verse of his day into a profound art. His travel diary The Narrow Road to the Deep North records a life spent walking Japan's roads in search of poetry.

Thiruvalluvar.bio: Tamil poet-saint traditionally credited with the Tirukkural, a classic of 1,330 couplets on virtue, wealth and love.

Orhan Pamuk.bio: Turkish novelist and Nobel laureate (2006). His novels, including My Name Is Red and Snow, blend Ottoman history with modern Istanbul.

W. B. Yeats.bio: William Butler Yeats was an Irish poet and a driving force of the Irish literary revival, co-founding Dublin's Abbey Theatre. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923, and poems such as The Second Coming and Sailing to Byzantium rank among the greatest of the 20th century.

Anaïs Nin.bio: Anaïs Nin was a French-born writer celebrated for her diaries, kept for more than sixty years and published from 1966 onward. Her lyrical exploration of the inner life and her friendships with writers such as Henry Miller made her a distinctive voice of 20th-century letters.

Joni Mitchell.bio: Joni Mitchell is a Canadian singer-songwriter and painter widely regarded as one of the greatest songwriters of the twentieth century. Her album Blue is a landmark of confessional songwriting, and her song 'Both Sides, Now' has been recorded by hundreds of artists.

Lin Yutang.bio: Lin Yutang was a Chinese writer and inventor who introduced Chinese philosophy and everyday life to Western readers with books such as My Country and My People and The Importance of Living. He championed a humorous, unhurried philosophy of life.

Harriet Tubman.bio: Born into slavery in Maryland, Harriet Tubman escaped in 1849 and then made some thirteen missions back into the South to rescue around seventy enslaved people through the Underground Railroad. During the Civil War she served the Union Army as a scout, spy and nurse.

Horace.bio: Horace was a leading Roman lyric poet under the emperor Augustus. His Odes, Satires and Ars Poetica gave European languages phrases such as carpe diem and continue to be quoted for their wisdom on moderation and contentment.

Audre Lorde.bio: Audre Lorde, who described herself as a 'Black, lesbian, mother, warrior, poet,' was an American writer whose poetry and essays confronted racism, sexism and homophobia head-on. Her essay collection Sister Outsider and The Cancer Journals remain foundational texts of modern feminism.

Charles Darwin.bio: Charles Darwin was an English naturalist whose theory of evolution by natural selection, set out in On the Origin of Species in 1859, revolutionised biology. He developed his ideas over two decades after his voyage aboard HMS Beagle around the world.

Frantz Fanon.bio: Martinican psychiatrist and philosopher whose books Black Skin, White Masks and The Wretched of the Earth became foundational texts on colonialism, race and liberation. He joined Algeria's independence struggle and died at thirty-six.

Mirza Ghalib.bio: Urdu and Persian poet of Mughal Delhi, regarded as the greatest master of the Urdu ghazal.

Václav Havel.bio: Václav Havel was a Czech playwright and dissident who became the first president of post-communist Czechoslovakia and then of the Czech Republic. His essays, especially The Power of the Powerless, articulated the moral resistance of living in truth under totalitarianism.

Emiliano Zapata.bio: Mexican revolutionary and leader of the Liberation Army of the South, whose Plan of Ayala demanded land for the peasants who worked it. A central figure of the Mexican Revolution, his cry of land and liberty endures in Mexican memory.

Sophocles.bio: Sophocles was an Athenian tragedian who wrote more than 120 plays, of which seven survive complete. Oedipus Rex and Antigone, his most famous works, set the pattern for Western tragedy.

Pythagoras.bio: Pythagoras was a Greek philosopher and mathematician who founded a religious and philosophical community in southern Italy. He is remembered for the theorem that bears his name and for teachings on number, harmony and the disciplined life.

Takeda Shingen.bio: Takeda Shingen was a Japanese daimyo of the Sengoku period, one of the era's most feared and capable warlords. His battle standard bore the famous Fūrinkazan motto from Sun Tzu: fast as the wind, silent as a forest, fierce as fire, immovable as a mountain.

Luther Standing Bear.bio: Oglala Lakota chief, educator, performer and author of Land of the Spotted Eagle. Educated at Carlisle Indian School, he wrote to correct the record about Lakota life, kinship and philosophy for white audiences.

Chiyo-ni.bio: Chiyo-ni was a Japanese haiku poet of the Edo period, one of the most celebrated women in the form. Her famous morning-glory haiku — giving up her well water rather than harm the vine — is known throughout Japan.

Stendhal.bio: Stendhal, the pen name of Marie-Henri Beyle, was a French novelist whose The Red and the Black and The Charterhouse of Parma pioneered psychological realism. Little appreciated in his lifetime, he predicted his fame would begin around 1880 — and was right.

José Martí.bio: Cuban poet, essayist and national hero who organised Cuba's independence movement and died fighting for it at Dos Ríos. His Versos sencillos (which gave the world 'Guantanamera') and essays shaped Latin American prose and thought.

Octavio Paz.bio: Mexican poet, essayist and diplomat, winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature (1990). His essay The Labyrinth of Solitude is a landmark meditation on Mexican identity, and his poetry bridges Mexican and European modernism.

André Gide.bio: André Gide was a French novelist and critic whose works, including The Immoralist and The Counterfeiters, explored freedom, desire and self-deception. He won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1947 and influenced generations of European writers.

Xunzi.bio: Xunzi was a Chinese Confucian philosopher of the late Warring States period. Unlike Mencius, he held that human nature is wayward and must be shaped by learning, ritual, and effort, and his writings stress disciplined study.

Wang Wei.bio: Wang Wei was a Tang-dynasty Chinese poet, painter, and Buddhist known for serene landscape poetry. Poems such as 'Deer Enclosure' distill a whole mountainside into a few quiet lines.

Yun Dong-ju.bio: Yun Dong-ju was a Korean poet who wrote lyrical, conscience-stricken verse under Japanese colonial rule. Arrested for independence activities, he died in a Fukuoka prison at twenty-eight; his poem 'Foreword' is known to every Korean schoolchild.

Liu Xiaobo.bio: Liu Xiaobo was a Chinese literary critic, writer, and human-rights activist who co-authored the Charter 08 manifesto. He was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 2010 while imprisoned, and his final statement was titled 'I Have No Enemies'.

Deng Xiaoping.bio: Deng Xiaoping was the Chinese leader who opened China to market reforms after 1978, lifting hundreds of millions out of poverty. His pragmatism is summed up in his saying that it does not matter whether a cat is black or white, as long as it catches mice.

Jin Yong.bio: Jin Yong was a Hong Kong novelist whose wuxia martial-arts epics, such as The Legend of the Condor Heroes, have been read by hundreds of millions across the Chinese-speaking world. He also co-founded the newspaper Ming Pao.

Francis Bacon.bio: Francis Bacon was an English philosopher, statesman and essayist who championed the empirical method of inquiry. His Essays and his plan for the reform of learning in the Novum Organum helped lay the groundwork of modern science.

Rigoberta Menchú.bio: K'iche' Maya activist from Guatemala who in 1992 became the first Indigenous person to receive the Nobel Peace Prize. Her testimony I, Rigoberta Menchú brought the struggles of Guatemala's Indigenous peoples to world attention.

Omar Khayyam.bio: Persian polymath — mathematician, astronomer and philosopher — whose Rubaiyat quatrains became world-famous in Edward FitzGerald's English translation.

Birago Diop.bio: Birago Diop was a Senegalese poet and storyteller who retold Wolof folktales in Tales of Amadou Koumba and celebrated Africa's oral tradition in poems such as 'Breaths'.

Chairil Anwar.bio: Chairil Anwar was an Indonesian poet whose fierce, modern verse transformed Indonesian literature before his death at twenty-six. His poem 'Aku' ('I'), ending with the wish to live another thousand years, is the country's most famous poem.

Edwidge Danticat.bio: Haitian-American novelist and memoirist, author of Breath, Eyes, Memory and the essay collection Create Dangerously. Her work bears witness to Haiti's history and to the lives of its diaspora.

Khaled Hosseini.bio: Afghan-American novelist, author of The Kite Runner and A Thousand Splendid Suns.

Emily Brontë.bio: Emily Brontë was an English novelist and poet whose single novel, Wuthering Heights, is a strange and powerful story of love and revenge on the Yorkshire moors. Intensely private, she published under the name Ellis Bell and died at thirty.

Milarepa.bio: Tibetan Buddhist yogi and poet. His hundred thousand songs are treasured across the Himalayas.

Florence Nightingale.bio: Florence Nightingale was an English social reformer and the founder of modern nursing, famed for organising care of wounded soldiers during the Crimean War. A gifted statistician, she used data to drive reforms in hospitals, sanitation and public health.

John Donne.bio: John Donne was an English poet and clergyman, the leading figure of the metaphysical poets. His love poems, sermons and prose meditations, including the Devotions upon Emergent Occasions, are famed for their wit and spiritual intensity.

Teresa of Ávila.bio: Teresa of Ávila was a Spanish Carmelite nun, mystic and reformer of the Carmelite order. Her spiritual classics The Interior Castle and The Way of Perfection, written with disarming directness, made her one of the most influential women writers of early modern Europe.

Jack Ma.bio: Jack Ma is a Chinese entrepreneur who co-founded Alibaba, one of the world's largest e-commerce companies, after a string of early rejections including dozens of failed job applications. He is known for blunt, resilient talks about failure and persistence.

Robert Browning.bio: Robert Browning was an English poet famed for his dramatic monologues, in which speakers reveal themselves in their own words. Married to the poet Elizabeth Barrett, he spent much of his life in Italy and published his masterpiece, The Ring and the Book, in 1868-69.

V. S. Naipaul.bio: Trinidad-born novelist who won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2001. Works such as A House for Mr Biswas and A Bend in the River examine colonial and postcolonial societies with unmatched precision.

Santoka Taneda.bio: Santoka Taneda was a Japanese Zen monk and free-verse haiku poet who wandered the country on foot for years, begging his way from temple to temple. His spare poems record mountains, rain, and sake with disarming honesty.

Amir Khusrau.bio: Persian poet, musician and scholar of Delhi, credited as a founder of qawwali and Hindustani classical music.

Shantideva.bio: Indian Buddhist monk and scholar of Nalanda. His Bodhicaryavatara is a classic guide to the bodhisattva path.

Paulo Coelho.bio: Brazilian lyricist and novelist whose novel The Alchemist became one of the best-selling books in history, translated into dozens of languages. His fables about following one's dreams have inspired readers on every continent.

Pablo Picasso.bio: Pablo Picasso was a Spanish artist who co-founded Cubism and reinvented his style across a career of nearly eighty years. Works such as Les Demoiselles d'Avignon and Guernica made him the most famous and influential artist of the 20th century.

Sri Ramakrishna.bio: Indian mystic and spiritual teacher of 19th-century Bengal. His teachings inspired the Ramakrishna Mission and Vedanta societies around the world.

Kim Gu.bio: Kim Gu was a leader of the Korean independence movement and head of the Provisional Government of the Republic of Korea in exile. His memoir Baekbeom Ilji dreams of a Korea that is not the richest or strongest nation, but the most beautiful.

Niccolò Machiavelli.bio: Niccolò Machiavelli was a Florentine diplomat and writer whose treatise The Prince analysed power with unsentimental realism. Long read as a manual of cunning statecraft, his works also include discourses defending republican government.
